title: RetroGraph: Retrosynthetic Planning with Graph Search

problem.claim: Retrosynthetic planning seeks a reaction pathway for synthesizing a target molecule and is usually modeled as a search problem.

gap.claim: Previous tree-based search methods independently revisit the same intermediate molecules, creating redundant and inefficient exploration.

contributions.claim: A graph-based search policy eliminates redundant exploration of intermediate molecules.
A graph neural network guides search over graphs.
The method searches batches of targets together and removes inter-target duplication in tree-based search.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Experiments on two datasets demonstrate the reported effectiveness of the method.
On the USPTO benchmark, the authors report a search success rate of 99.47%.
On the USPTO benchmark, the authors report improvement over previous state-of-the-art performance by 2.6 points.

narrative_sequence.summary: Retrosynthetic planning is an important chemistry and drug-discovery task modeled as search.
Data-driven methods have shown promising results, but tree-based methods repeatedly treat the same intermediate molecules independently.
Repeated intermediate exploration makes search inefficient.
The proposed approach uses graph search, a graph neural network, and batch target search to reduce redundant exploration.
Experiments on two datasets report effectiveness, including a 99.47% USPTO search success rate and a 2.6-point advance over prior state of the art.

source_observation.claim: Intermediate molecules are revisited across search paths, causing redundant exploration.

interpretation.claim: Representing shared intermediate states explicitly may improve search efficiency.

application.claim: For search problems with repeated states, consider graph-based state sharing instead of independent tree branches.

exception.claim: Graph search may introduce additional complexity compared with tree search.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the two datasets beyond the USPTO benchmark.
The abstract does not describe the experimental protocol, baselines, or statistical validation.
